extractions.value: Clinical features (axial and proximal stiffness, stimulus-sensitive painful cramps), EMG showing continuous motor unit activity suppressed by diazepam, and response to diazepam. The authors state the features fulfilled the diagnostic criteria of SMS proposed by Lorish et al.
extractions.quote: The above features fulfilled the diagnostic criteria of SMS proposed by Lorish et al [2]

This patient had an axial and proximal stiffness starting from the lower back with a progressive involvement of the neck and limbs. The stiffness was very sensitive to external stimulation, particularly any sudden movement, which frequently induced a painful cramp.

Autoantibodies directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD antibodies) ... can be found in the serum and cerebrospinal fluid of 60% of patients with SMS [7]; however, this investigation was not available to the authors.
EMG investigation revealed continuous muscle activity that was dramatically suppressed in response to high dose diazepam.
The therapeutic response to diazepam ... is so effective and characteristic, it is the most useful diagnostic criterion for SMS [2].

Although Isaacs' syndrome is associated with similar continuous motor unit activity on EMG recording, the stiffness is different from that seen in this patient ... Tetanus also presents with generalized muscle spasms, but trismus and a history of injury or of drug abuse are usually present ... Myotonia differs in specific EMG pattern ... The Schwartz-Jampel syndrome has similar EMG features, but patients often have a distinctive facial expression, bone deformities, joint contracture, and myotonia. These features were not found in this patient. Generalized dystonia may be confused with SMS, but the earlier onset, earlier twisting of the distal limb muscles, and positive family history are different from SMS.

extractions.value: First report of stiff-man syndrome in a Taiwanese patient. The patient had a left S1 radiculopathy due to L5-S1 disc protrusion, which was treated with discectomy before the SMS diagnosis. The stiffness subsided during normal sleep. The patient was unable to drive a car due to limited neck mobility. Neck and back flexion were limited to about 35° and 30° respectively.
